title: Marking a Cell and Its Descendants

scenes.tts: A neuron has no label saying where it came from. So how do you find out? A birth date marks one cohort of cells. A lineage is one family. To follow one, write a mark into a cell's own DNA. Then every descendant carries it. The tool that does this is an enzyme called Cree recombinase.

scenes.visual: Mystery cell with question marks; a green mark is written into its DNA; the cell divides and the mark appears in every daughter; a Cre chip arrives.
scenes.narration: A neuron has no label saying where it came from. So how do you find out? A birth date marks one cohort of cells. A lineage is one family. To follow one, write a mark into a cell's own DNA. Then every descendant carries it. The tool that does this is an enzyme called Cre recombinase.

scenes.tts: Start with the gene for a fluorescent protein. A reporter like this shows where a cell is. In front of it, place a transcriptional stop signal. Put a lox P site on each side of that stop. Each site is a short DNA sequence, 34 base pairs long. This is a Cree-dependent reporter. While the stop is in place, the gene is not read.

scenes.visual: A DNA strip is built: gene, stop in front, loxP sites around the stop; the strip is dark.

scenes.tts: Now Cree recombinase appears in a cell. It deletes the stop that the sites flank. The reporter is read, and the cell glows. Cree is made from a promoter active in one cell type. Only cells that make Cree delete the stop. Their neighbors stay dark.
scenes.caption: Now Cre recombinase appears in a cell. It deletes the stop that the sites flank. The reporter is read, and the cell glows. Cre is made from a promoter active in one cell type. Only cells that make Cre delete the stop. Their neighbors stay dark.
scenes.visual: Six cells with the reporter strip; Cre appears in two, their stops are deleted and they glow; the others stay dark.
scenes.narration: Now Cre recombinase appears in a cell. It deletes the stop that the sites flank. The reporter is read, and the cell glows. Cre is made from a promoter active in one cell type. Only cells that make Cre delete the stop. Their neighbors stay dark.

scenes.tts: Now that cell divides. The deletion is in its DNA, so both daughters inherit it. The reporter is read in that cell and in every one of its descendants from then on. The marking is permanent. That is exactly what lineage tracing requires.

scenes.visual: A glowing cell divides into a growing family tree; every cell glows.

scenes.tts: Cree can also remove a gene. Flank an important part of a gene with lox P sites. That allele is called floxed, and it works normally. Supply Cree from a promoter active in one cell type, and the gene is deleted there alone. A whole-body knockout cannot tell you which tissue mattered. For timing, fuse Cree to a modified estrogen receptor. Then the deletion waits for the drug tamoxifen.

scenes.visual: Two cells with a gene; loxP sites flank a part; Cre enters one cell and the part is cut out there only.
scenes.narration: Cre can also remove a gene. Flank an important part of a gene with loxP sites. That allele is called floxed, and it works normally. Supply Cre from a promoter active in one cell type, and the gene is deleted there alone. A whole-body knockout cannot tell you which tissue mattered. scenes.tts: One trap. A reporter cross tells you where Cree acted. It does not tell you where the floxed gene was lost. The two lox-flanked targets recombine independently. Drivers can be leaky or mosaic. Protein made before the cut persists. So measure the loss itself. A reporter shows where Cree acted, not where the gene is gone.
